newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel opens Jerusalem tunnel and political row.
newsitem.headline: Israel opens Jerusalem tunnel and political row.

text.p: Israel's right-wing government opened a tunnel near Islam's third holiest site on Tuesday, igniting Palestinian protests reminiscent of the intifada and further souring relations with Arab states.

Palestinians clashed with police after workmen under cover of night and heavy police guard punched a second entrance through a stonewall to a tourist tunnel beside Jerusalem's Temple Mount, a site holy to Jews and Moslems.

Police said they fired rubber bullets to disperse youths throwing stones and bottles and briefly evacuated Jewish worshippers from the Wailing Wall after stones were hurled from the Temple Mount above. Youths also set alight vehicles. Several were arrested. No injuries were reported.
Palestinian President Yasser Arafat called the tunnel a "crime" against the religious status quo in the disputed city, and a breach of the foundering Israeli-PLO peace accord.
In Cairo, the Arab League said Israel had enraged Moslems worldwide and risked triggering widespread unrest.
In London, visiting Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu defended the move.

"(It is) a decision I am very proud that we are implementing," he told reporters on his plane. "Whoever has been in the Wailing Wall tunnel -- I was there a year ago -- could not help but feel the emotion to the depths of his soul...we are touching the rock of our existence," he said, referring to the site's association with the rock upon which Abraham offered Isaac in sacrifice.
In Jerusalem, authorities said the decision to open a second entrance on the Via Dolorosa, Christ's traditional route to Calvary, was taken by the ousted Labour administration but postponed.

"It must be emphasied that this tunnel has nothing to do with any religious site, and therefore has no ramifications whatsoever for holy sites for Christians or for Moslems," Jerusalem's right-wing mayor Ehud Olmert told a news conference, convened as protests spread across the city's Arab Eastern sector.
Palestinian leaders called for a second day of strikes and a demonstration after Moslem noon prayers on Wednesday.
The 488-metre (500-yard)-long tunnel, which exposes the Herodian foundations of the Wailing Wall, has been open for some time with only one entry and exit point in the Jewish Quarter of the Old City.
"This is a crime, a big crime against our religious and holy places," Arafat said in Palestinian-ruled Gaza. "This (is) Israeli madness to change the features of Jerusalem," Arafat told reporters.

A joint statement by the PLO and Palestinian parliament called on foreign governments and institutions to defend Jerusalem against what it called a "Zionist, Israeli plot to Judaise the holy city, al-Aqsa mosque and the rest of Islamic and Christian holy places."

Israel said the new entrance would allow tourists easier access to archaeological sites beneath the Wailing Wall, Judaism's holiest site. The Israeli government said the second entrance would allow 400,000 tourists a year to use the tunnel whereas now only 70,000 a year have been able to squeeze through the metre-wide opening which serves as both entrance and exit.
The Temple Mount, known to Moslems as Haram al-Sharif, houses the Dome of the Rock and al-Aqsa mosques. It is a flashpoint in the Israeli-Palestinian struggle.
